title: The duty is the overlay, not a makeweight
paras: Right — heritage. The statutory duties overlay the whole decision, not a makeweight. Where development affects a listed building or its setting, you must have special regard to preserving the building, its setting, and its features of special architectural or historic interest. In a conservation area, the parallel duty is special attention to preserving or enhancing the area's character or appearance. Not ordinary considerations to trade away — the courts give them considerable importance and weight.

'Preserving' means to do no harm — that's South Lakeland. Leave the building, setting or area unharmed and the duty is satisfied even if you add nothing; harm them and it isn't. The duty is negative — it won't compel enhancement — but it bites against harm; and because the conservation-area duty is in the alternative, preserve or enhance, a scheme doing neither can fail where the context called for one. Barnwell sets up a strong presumption against permission for anything harming a listed building's setting, holding even where the harm is less than substantial — Forge Field added that any benefit relied on to outweigh it must be of commensurate force. So give the harm its statutory weight before balancing.

Don't confuse the duty with national heritage policy. Mordue says working properly through the policy's heritage paragraphs generally discharges the duty too — the Mordue shortcut — but that's a presumption of compliance, not a substitute; apply policy mechanically while forgetting the duty and the decision is vulnerable as an error of law. So identify the duty expressly, apply the presumption, then balance. And one parallel regime: works to a scheduled monument need scheduled monument consent — separate from listed building consent and planning permission, not granted by the council — but its significance and setting stay material to any planning decision affecting them.

title: Significance is the whole game
paras: Significance is the whole game — the value of a heritage asset to this and future generations for its heritage interest, from both fabric and setting. You can't assess harm to a significance you haven't established, so a Heritage Statement that hasn't pinned it down hasn't started. The recurring failing is describing what an asset is — date, materials, grade — instead of why it matters.

National policy gives four interests: archaeological, architectural, artistic and historic. Architectural is design, craftsmanship, quality as architecture; historic is the illustrative or associative links to past people, events and ways of life; artistic is design or decorative quality; archaeological is the potential of fabric or ground to yield evidence about the past. Most assets carry more than one, and they can pull different ways — a plain building of high historic interest may have little architectural quality, and you say so rather than flatten it to one verdict. Historic England's Conservation Principles run a parallel set — evidential, historical, aesthetic, communal — mapping onto the same idea; that's under review, so check its status, but the habit is the point: identify what carries the significance element by element, and mark what's neutral or intrusive.

Keep it proportionate — no more than enough to understand the proposal's impact on significance. A grade one church and its designed setting warrant a fuller statement than a modest unlisted building in a conservation area, and the effort goes where the proposal bites — a thin statement for an important asset and bloated boilerplate for a modest one are equal and opposite failures. What you want is a Statement of Significance identifying the elements that carry significance and the contribution of setting — the document the whole assessment stands on.

title: The list description is not the significance
paras: The list entry is not the significance — treating it as the definition is a common, costly trap inspectors return to. The entry describes the asset and explains, often briefly, why it was listed: a finding aid, not a definition. Listing protects the whole building and can reach beyond it, so the significance is often far wider than the entry suggests.

On extent: listing covers the entire building, inside and out; any object or structure fixed to it; and any object or structure within the curtilage that, though not fixed, has been part of the land since before 1948. So an interior the entry never mentions, or a curtilage barn, wall, gatepier or outbuilding, may be substantial and fully protected even where the description is silent. Assuming an interior or curtilage structure is unprotected is a frequent, serious error — and the curtilage tests cross-refer to the lawful development and curtilage material.

So establish significance from the entry and well beyond it: the Historic Environment Record, historic Ordnance Survey and tithe maps, archives, old photographs, earlier assessments. And above all, inspect inside and out — much of what carries significance, a historic plan form, roof structure, surviving joinery or plaster, is invisible from the street and absent from the entry. Inspectors treat the description as a starting point; rely on it as the definition and your assessment gets little weight.

title: Setting is not just the view
paras: Setting is not just the view. It's the surroundings in which an asset is experienced — its extent isn't fixed, and it isn't only visual. Historic, functional, designed and experiential relationships all feed the significance an asset draws from setting. Land can matter with no direct view, and land in full sight may contribute nothing. The question is never whether the asset can be seen — it's whether, and how, the surroundings contribute to its significance.

Catesby confirmed that: setting isn't limited to visual or physical connection, and historic, social and economic links can contribute — but it cautioned that a merely remote or conceptual connection may contribute little or nothing. Setting isn't boundless: identify the real contribution, not the widest circle. An over-tight setting stopping at the red line misses a genuine contribution; an over-generous one sweeps in unrelated land and invites the answer that the link is too tenuous.

For method, use Historic England's staged approach to setting — five steps, in order. Identify the assets affected and their settings. Assess whether and how the setting contributes to each asset's significance — the experience in the round, approaches, key views, the relationship as you move through the landscape. Assess the proposal's effect on that contribution. Look for ways to maximise enhancement and avoid or minimise harm. And make and document the decision. Inspectors expect that reasoning worked through, not a bare assertion of visibility. Check the current edition, but the staged approach is settled.

title: Harm is to significance, not to bricks
paras: Harm is to significance, not to bricks. Works to fabric, development in a setting, the loss of a contributing element, incremental and cumulative change — all can harm significance, and it's the effect on significance you assess and locate, not the intervention you count. A big intervention in low-significance fabric may cause little harm; a small one in the most significant fabric a great deal. Policy sorts it into three: no harm; less than substantial harm; substantial harm or total loss.

Substantial harm is a high threshold, and the most litigated point in the field. Bedford is the marker: an impact so serious that very much, if not all, of the significance is drained away — not merely 'considerable', and not reached just because an important asset is affected. Total demolition, or works that gut a building's historic interest, is substantial harm or total loss; a well-designed extension, or development in part of a wider setting, rarely crosses the line. So most real-world harm — including plenty that's serious — falls into the less than substantial band, which is why handling it correctly matters.

Keep it honest by locating the harm precisely instead of reaching for a label: no harm; less than substantial and where on the band, lower, middle or upper; or substantial. The three carry very different policy consequences, so inflating ordinary harm to 'substantial' to prop up a refusal, and deflating real harm below the line to ease a grant, both come apart under scrutiny. And assess setting and cumulative effects alongside direct works — in a conservation area especially, incremental loss across many small approvals is a real, recognised form of harm, not a reason to treat each application in isolation.

title: “Less than substantial” is not “less than substantial weight”
paras: 'Less than substantial' is not 'less than substantial weight' — the most misunderstood point in the field. The phrase only tells you which policy test applies; it says nothing about how heavily the harm weighs. Less than substantial harm still attracts great weight under policy, and considerable importance and weight under the statutory duty. Reading the label as a signal the harm is minor loses more heritage appeals than any other error.

Policy gives great weight to conserving a designated asset — and the more important the asset, the greater that weight. Grade one and grade two star listed buildings, scheduled monuments, protected wreck sites, registered battlefields, grade one and grade two star registered parks and gardens, and World Heritage Sites are all assets of the highest significance, and harm to them carries greater weight. That requirement applies whether the harm is substantial or less than substantial — the lower band doesn't switch it off. And any harm to, or loss of, a designated asset's significance needs clear and convincing justification, which a general appeal to benefit won't meet.

The courts shut the fallacy down directly. Bramshill held that categorising harm and striking the heritage balance are matters of planning judgement — but that less than substantial harm is not to be equated with a less than substantial planning objection. So state both the category of harm and the weight you give it, and calibrate that weight to the asset's importance — a grade two and a grade one aren't treated alike.

title: Two balances, and how not to double-count
paras: Two balances, and don't double-count between them. The internal heritage balance is a policy test on the heritage harm alone — that harm against the public benefits bearing on it. The overall balance then weighs the whole planning case, heritage included. Substantial and less than substantial harm run different internal tests. And because the heritage harm already carries great weight, you must not count the same harm, or the same benefit, twice as it moves from one balance to the other.

For substantial harm or total loss the internal test is strict: refuse unless it's shown either that the harm is necessary to achieve substantial public benefits that outweigh it, or that four alternative conditions are all met — that the nature of the asset prevents all reasonable uses; that no viable use can be found in the medium term through appropriate marketing; that conservation by grant funding or not-for-profit ownership is demonstrably impossible; and that the harm is outweighed by the benefit of bringing the site back into use. Such harm should be wholly exceptional for the highest-significance assets, exceptional for the rest. For less than substantial harm the test is different: weigh the harm against the public benefits of the proposal, including, where appropriate, securing optimum viable use. Run the wrong test and that's a self-inflicted error.

Public benefits can be heritage benefits — securing long-term conservation, or revealing or better presenting significance — or wider ones: housing including affordable housing, economic activity, environmental gains, regeneration, public access. But they must be genuine public benefits, not private gain; must flow from the proposal; and must be deliverable, not speculative. Since the harm carries great weight, a modest benefit won't readily outweigh even less than substantial harm to an important asset. Two concepts recur: optimum viable use is the use doing least harm to significance while keeping the asset viably in use, not necessarily the most profitable — securing it is itself a public benefit, and failing to secure any viable use can threaten the asset. And enabling development is development normally refused, allowed because it secures the future of an asset that can't otherwise be funded — governed by Historic England's tests and safeguards against abuse.

The heritage conclusion then feeds the overall balance, which this app hands to the Decision-Making area. The critical interaction: designated-heritage policy can give a clear reason for refusal, and where it does, it disengages the tilted balance — so a scheme that would otherwise ride the presumption in favour of sustainable development, because the authority can't show a five-year housing land supply, can still be refused on heritage grounds. Run each balance once, on its own terms, and never count the same harm or benefit in both.

title: Archaeology, and why recording is not a cure
paras: Where a site has archaeological potential, understand the significance of any remains before determination — desk-based assessment, and where that's not enough, field evaluation like geophysical survey or trial trenching — so the decision is informed, not deferred. And recording is not mitigation: it offsets, in part, the loss of knowledge otherwise destroyed with the remains, but does nothing for the loss of significance itself. Don't accept a Statement presenting recording as if it neutralised the harm.

The order of operations is what inspectors and courts hold firm on. Where a site has or may have archaeological interest, national policy requires the desk-based assessment first, and field evaluation where that's insufficient, so significance is understood before determination. Deferring it to a post-permission condition puts the decision the wrong way round — you can't weigh harm to a significance you haven't established, and a condition requiring evaluation 'to inform the development' is no substitute for evaluation that informs whether to permit it at all.

Preservation in situ is the preferred outcome for remains of significance. Where harm or loss is unavoidable and justified, recording and analysis may be secured by condition — but the ability to record is not a factor in deciding whether the loss should be permitted. And watch the status of non-designated archaeology: non-designated assets generally get a balanced judgement weighing scale of harm against significance, but non-designated archaeological remains of demonstrably equivalent significance to a scheduled monument get a distinct, more protective approach — identify them as such rather than defaulting to the ordinary balance.

title: The method, step 1: identify the assets
paras: Right — the method: a repeatable six-step sequence, and the discipline is the order, because each step gates the next. The doctrine above supplies the principles; the overall and tilted balances go to the Decision-Making area. Step one: identify every heritage asset the proposal could affect.

List them all — designated: listed buildings with their grade, conservation areas, scheduled monuments, registered parks and gardens, registered battlefields, World Heritage Sites; and non-designated, whether on a local list or turned up during the application. Include assets affected only through their setting, which needn't be on or next to the site. Interrogate the datasets rather than the red line — the national heritage list, the Historic Environment Record, the local list, the constraints map — and produce a schedule: each asset, its grade, and whether affected directly, through setting, or both.

title: The method, step 2: understand significance
paras: Step two: understand significance. For each asset, say why it matters — which heritage interests apply, how much different elements and fabric contribute, and what the setting adds. State it proportionately to importance and go beyond the list description, using the Historic Environment Record, historic maps and archives, and inspection inside and out. The output is a proportionate Statement of Significance identifying the elements that carry significance and the contribution of setting — the document every later step relies on. The errors: describing what the asset is not why it matters; treating the list entry as the significance; disproportion either way.

title: The method, step 3: assess the effect
paras: Step three: assess the effect. Identify precisely where and how the proposal touches significance — works to fabric, development in the setting, loss of a contributing element, cumulative change — then locate the harm: no harm; less than substantial and where on the spectrum; or substantial or total loss. Assess setting and cumulative effects, not just direct works. The errors: assessing damage to fabric instead of harm to significance; letting the label do the work without locating the harm; and inflating to substantial — a high bar, remember Bedford — or deflating below the line.

title: The method, step 4: apply the weight
paras: Step four: apply the weight, as two distinct moves. Give great weight to the asset's conservation, scaled by importance, whether the harm is substantial or less than substantial. Then, separately, discharge the statutory duty: give the harm considerable importance and weight and apply the strong presumption — Barnwell and Forge Field — and require clear and convincing justification for any harm. The errors: treating less than substantial harm as low weight; skipping the duty because national policy was cited — remember Mordue; and giving a grade two the same weight as a grade one.

title: The method, step 5: run the correct balance
paras: Step five: run the correct internal test. Substantial harm or total loss runs the strict test — refuse unless the harm is necessary for substantial public benefits that outweigh it, or all four alternative limbs are met. Less than substantial harm runs the weighing test — the harm against the public benefits of the proposal, including securing optimum viable use. Identify benefits that are genuine, public and deliverable, weigh them against harm that already carries great weight, and feed the conclusion into the overall balance. The errors: the wrong internal test; inflating benefits or counting private gain; double-counting the same harm or benefit across the two balances; and forgetting that heritage can supply a clear reason for refusal that switches off the tilt.

title: The method, step 6: avoid, reduce, document
paras: Step six: avoid, reduce, document. Return to design and mitigation to avoid or minimise harm and maximise enhancement — the closing step of the staged setting approach. Secure what you can by condition or obligation — recording and analysis, method statements, materials, management — then record the judgement clearly, in reasoned sequence, because the discipline of writing it is the discipline of making it. The errors: presenting recording as if it mitigated the loss of significance; using conditions to defer the significance assessment that should have preceded determination; and a conclusion that asserts an outcome without showing the reasoning.

title: Worked: extension to a grade II listed building
paras: A worked example — an extension to a grade two listed building, illustrative not real. A two-storey rear extension to a grade two, early nineteenth-century farmhouse, removing a later twentieth-century lean-to and forming a new opening through a historic rear wall, the interior keeping its historic plan form and principal joinery. The significance is a modest but intact vernacular farmhouse — symmetrical front, historic fabric and roof form, a legible plan; the lean-to is a neutral-to-negative accretion, and the setting contributes modestly.

The opening removes historic rear fabric and slightly erodes the plan's legibility, and the extension must stay subservient; removing the lean-to is a heritage benefit. So the harm is less than substantial, lower-to-middle of the band, carrying its proper statutory weight and needing clear and convincing justification. On the less-than-substantial test, the benefits are modest but genuine — the house's continued optimum viable use for modern family living, plus losing the lean-to. It's finely poised and turns on design: minimise the opening, place it in less significant fabric, make it reversible, match the materials, and the benefits can outweigh the reduced harm. So less than substantial harm capable of being outweighed on conditions — matching materials, joinery details, a reversible opening, the lean-to removal secured — a defensible conditional grant, where a larger or more damaging opening would tip it to refusal.

title: Worked: development in a listed building’s setting
paras: A second example — development in a listed building's setting. Nine dwellings in an open field adjoining a grade two star medieval parish church whose isolated, landmark rural setting contributes strongly to its significance — the church reads as a landmark across open fields on the approach to the village.

On the staged approach: the setting plainly contributes, and the development would enclose the open foreground and erode both the church's landmark quality and the church-and-countryside relationship from key views and approaches. So the harm is less than substantial but toward the upper end, precisely because the asset is of the highest significance — great weight, lifted by the grade two star status, the more important the asset the greater the weight, plus clear and convincing justification. The benefit is a modest housing contribution including affordable homes, and against upper-end harm to a highest-significance asset carrying great weight it doesn't clearly outweigh. And designated-heritage policy gives a clear reason for refusal that disengages the tilted balance — even if housing land supply is short. So refusal is defensible, and heritage switches off the tilt. A clearer case than the finely poised extension.

title: Worked: loss in a conservation area
paras: A third example — loss in a conservation area. Demolition of an unlisted but locally distinctive Victorian villa that makes a positive contribution to a conservation area, replaced by a larger apartment building, in a street that's already seen incremental change. The significance in issue is the character and appearance of the conservation area; the villa's scale, materials and rhythm reinforce its Victorian character, so its loss is harm to the area.

Losing a positive-contribution building erodes that character, the replacement's scale and design matter, and there's a cumulative dimension — death by a thousand cuts. The harm is less than substantial, because losing a single building rarely drains very much of an area's significance — the Bedford high bar again — but it's real, and the cumulative context sharpens it. Great weight to the area's conservation, the duty of special attention, and the reminder from South Lakeland that preserving means doing no harm: a harmful scheme does not preserve.

On the less-than-substantial test — informed by the policy that losing a positive-contribution element is treated as substantial or less than substantial harm accordingly — the benefits are additional housing and, if the villa genuinely can't be viably retained, a viable use of the site. This is where it turns: the evidential burden is on the applicant to show retention isn't viable and that the replacement would preserve or enhance the area. On robust viability evidence and a high-quality replacement, the benefits may tip it; on weak evidence, the loss plus cumulative erosion outweighs a general housing benefit. So it's finely balanced and evidence-dependent — refusal where retention is viable and the replacement unremarkable, a possible conditional grant where unviability is robustly shown and the replacement genuinely enhances the area.

title: What appeals consistently show
paras: Finally — what appeals consistently show, from Planning Inspectorate casework: practice, not law. Inspectors expect significance established clearly before harm — jump to harm without it and you get little weight. 'Less than substantial' isn't trivial: it routinely gets great weight and considerable importance and weight, with the harm located on the spectrum, not left to the label. And public benefits are scrutinised — genuine, public and deliverable, weighed against harm carrying great weight, so modest benefits rarely outweigh harm to an important asset.

Setting harm is frequently decisive, and the staged setting approach is expected, not a bare visual analysis; the list description is a starting point, not the definition of significance; cumulative erosion of conservation-area character carries real weight where evidenced — the thousand cuts; and recording is not accepted as mitigation for lost significance. The pattern: inspectors reward rigour — significance established, harm located and weighed at its proper weight, benefits tested — and are unimpressed by labels, assertion, and benefit claimed but not delivered.
